question: In New York, a closing attorney who receives buyer or seller funds in connection with a closing is generally required to hold those funds in what type of account, separate from the attorney's personal or business funds?
choice_a: An attorney trust/escrow account (such as an IOLA account), governed by the New York Rules of Professional Conduct -- a separate obligation from a broker's escrow duties under 19 NYCRR Section 175.1
choice_b: The attorney's ordinary personal checking account
choice_c: The buyer's own personal bank account, with the attorney merely observing
choice_d: No separate account is required as long as the attorney keeps a mental note of whose money is whose
explanation: New York attorneys handling client/closing funds must maintain them in a dedicated trust/escrow account (commonly an IOLA account) under the Rules of Professional Conduct, segregated from personal/business funds and from any other client's funds -- a parallel, attorney-specific fiduciary duty distinct from (but structurally similar to) a broker's escrow obligations under 19 NYCRR Section 175.1.
source_note: NY Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.15, attorney trust/IOLA account requirements)

question: Since New York's remote online notarization (RON) framework took effect (codified at Executive Law Section 135-c), which statement best describes its effect on New York real estate closings?
choice_a: A registered New York electronic notary public, while physically located in New York, may notarize closing documents remotely via secure live audio-video technology with identity verification -- supplementing, not replacing, New York's traditional in-person closing custom
choice_b: All New York real estate closings must now be conducted entirely online with no attorney involvement
choice_c: Remote notarization eliminates the need for any identity verification of the signer
choice_d: New York never permits any form of remote or electronic notarization
explanation: New York's RON law (effective January 31, 2023, Executive Law Section 135-c) allows a registered New York electronic notary, while physically located in the state, to notarize documents remotely using secure audio-video technology and identity verification -- a modernization that gives closings additional flexibility without abolishing New York's underlying attorney-driven, document-intensive closing custom.
source_note: NY Executive Law Section 135-c (remote online notarization, effective Jan. 31, 2023)

question: Where are New York residential closings customarily held?
choice_a: At a private location such as the buyer's attorney's office, the lender's attorney's office, or the title company's office -- not at a government office or courthouse
choice_b: Exclusively at the county clerk's office
choice_c: Exclusively at the Department of State's Albany office
choice_d: Exclusively at a courthouse before a judge
explanation: Consistent with New York's private, attorney-negotiated closing custom, closings are customarily held at a private office -- often the buyer's attorney, the lender's attorney, or the title company -- rather than at any government office; the deed and mortgage are separately brought to the county clerk (or filed via ACRIS in New York City) for recording after closing.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated NY real estate closing-practice convention

question: How does New York treat 'closing protection letters' (CPLs) -- a document common in many other states in which a title insurer agrees to indemnify a lender for certain misconduct or errors by the title agent at closing?
choice_a: New York generally prohibits title insurers from issuing standard closing protection letters for New York property; instead, a title insurer may issue a more limited agent authorization letter confined to the agent's authorized acts
choice_b: New York requires every closing to include a closing protection letter, with no exceptions
choice_c: Closing protection letters are unique to New York and unavailable anywhere else in the country
choice_d: Closing protection letters have nothing to do with title insurance and are issued only by mortgage lenders
explanation: Unlike most other states, New York title insurers are prohibited from issuing the standard closing protection letter to lenders for New York real property (per NY Department of Financial Services guidance); a title insurer may instead issue a more limited agent authorization letter covering the title agent's authorized acts -- a distinctive feature of New York title insurance regulation.
source_note: NY DFS Circular Letter No. 18 (1992) and OGC Opinion No. 05-12-24 (closing protection letters prohibited for NY property)

question: What is 'gap coverage' in the context of a New York title insurance policy, and how routinely is it provided?
choice_a: Coverage protecting against liens or other matters recorded during the 'gap' between the closing/title search cutoff and the actual recording of the deed/mortgage -- provided as a matter of course in New York, unlike in some other states
choice_b: Coverage for gaps in a fence line between neighboring properties
choice_c: A discount applied when there is a gap of several years between two prior sales of the property
choice_d: Coverage that only applies if the buyer pays an additional, rarely-purchased endorsement
explanation: New York title insurance customarily provides 'gap coverage' as a matter of course, protecting against intervening liens or encumbrances that could be recorded during the gap between the last title search/closing and the actual recording of the new deed and mortgage -- an important protection given the practical delay between signing documents and getting them on record.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title insurance industry practice (recording-gap coverage)

question: How are title insurance premium rates generally determined in New York?
choice_a: They are set according to rate schedules filed with and regulated by the New York State Department of Financial Services (informed by rating organizations such as TIRSA), rather than freely negotiated case-by-case
choice_b: Each title company may charge any amount it wishes with no regulatory oversight
choice_c: Title insurance premiums are fixed nationally by the federal government
choice_d: Title insurance in New York has no premium at all -- coverage is free
explanation: New York title insurance premiums are governed by rate schedules filed with the state Department of Financial Services (informed by rating organizations such as the Title Insurance Rate Service Association, TIRSA), rather than being freely negotiated on a case-by-case basis the way some other closing costs may be.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title insurance rate-regulation industry practice (DFS-filed rates; TIRSA)

question: What is the role of a 'title closer' at a New York real estate closing?
choice_a: A title company representative who works to narrow the gap between the last title search and the closing, notarizes documents, collects good funds, and ensures the deed and mortgage are promptly sent for recording
choice_b: An attorney who represents the buyer in contract negotiations
choice_c: A government employee who approves the sale price
choice_d: A broker who negotiates the final purchase price at the closing table
explanation: The title closer, typically an employee of the title insurance company or agency, works to narrow the gap between the last title search and closing, notarizes closing documents, collects the closing (good) funds, and coordinates prompt recording of the deed and mortgage after closing to minimize gap risk.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title-closing industry practice (title closer's role)

question: In addition to examining the recorded chain of title, what other searches does a New York title company customarily run against the seller and buyer before closing?
choice_a: Name searches for judgments, federal tax liens, and bankruptcy filings that could attach to a party personally and affect the property
choice_b: A search of the buyer's credit card statements
choice_c: A search of the seller's tax returns for the past ten years
choice_d: No searches beyond the recorded deed are ever performed
explanation: Beyond the recorded chain of title, a title company customarily runs name searches against the seller (and often the buyer) for judgments, federal tax liens, and bankruptcy filings -- off-record matters that could nonetheless attach to and affect the property being conveyed.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title examination industry practice (judgment/lien/bankruptcy name searches)

question: What is a title 'bring-down' (or continuation) search, performed at or near the time of closing?
choice_a: An updated search that brings the title examination current through the closing date, to catch any new liens, judgments, or conveyances recorded since the original title report/commitment was issued
choice_b: A search that looks back 100 years into the property's ownership history for the first time
choice_c: A survey performed by a licensed land surveyor
choice_d: A background check on the broker's license status
explanation: A bring-down (or continuation) search updates the title examination as close to the closing date as practicable, so that the title company can confirm no new liens, judgments, or conveyances have been recorded since the original title report/commitment, before issuing the final title policy.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title examination industry practice (bring-down/continuation search)

question: When an owner's title policy and a lender's title policy are issued simultaneously in the same New York transaction, what is generally true about the pricing of the lender's policy?
choice_a: The lender's policy is generally issued at a reduced 'simultaneous issue' rate, rather than its own full, stand-alone premium, because the owner's policy premium already covers most of the underlying risk
choice_b: The lender's policy always costs exactly double the owner's policy
choice_c: Simultaneous issuance is illegal in New York
choice_d: The owner's policy becomes free if a lender's policy is also purchased
explanation: New York's filed title insurance rate schedules generally provide a reduced 'simultaneous issue' rate for a lender's policy issued at the same time as an owner's policy on the same property, since much of the underlying title risk is already covered by the owner's policy premium -- keeping the combined cost lower than pricing each policy independently.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title insurance rate practice (simultaneous-issue rate for concurrently issued owner's/lender's policies)

question: If a minor title issue surfaces shortly before closing (such as a small unpaid judgment or an open building violation) that cannot be fully resolved by the closing date, what tool might a title company use to allow the closing to proceed?
choice_a: 'Insuring over' the issue -- agreeing to omit or except the item from an objection while the parties place funds in an escrow holdback (or obtain an indemnity) to resolve it after closing
choice_b: The closing must always be canceled permanently with no alternative
choice_c: The buyer must simply ignore the issue with no protection of any kind
choice_d: The title company must always refuse to issue any policy if any issue, however small, remains open
explanation: Rather than delaying or canceling a closing over a minor, curable title issue, a title company will often agree to 'insure over' it -- issuing the policy while the parties escrow sufficient funds (a holdback) or obtain an indemnity to guarantee the issue gets resolved (e.g., a lien paid off and satisfaction recorded) shortly after closing.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title insurance/closing industry practice (insuring over an exception with an escrow holdback)

question: What is an 'affidavit of title' (or similarly named no-lien/no-judgment affidavit) that a seller commonly signs at a New York closing?
choice_a: A sworn statement by the seller confirming matters such as no undisclosed liens, judgments, or parties in possession, and no recent improvements that could support an unfiled mechanic's lien -- relied on by the title company in issuing its policy
choice_b: A document that transfers legal title by itself, without a deed
choice_c: A form only relevant to commercial, never residential, transactions
choice_d: A document the buyer, not the seller, is required to sign
explanation: A seller's affidavit of title (sometimes called a no-lien or no-judgment affidavit) is a sworn statement addressing matters like undisclosed liens, judgments, parties in possession, and recent unpaid improvement work that could support a mechanic's lien -- information the title company relies on, together with its search, in agreeing to issue its policy.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY title closing industry practice (seller's affidavit of title)

question: How is ownership of a New York cooperative apartment legally transferred at closing, in contrast to a house or condo?
choice_a: By assignment of the seller's shares of stock in the cooperative corporation, together with assignment of the proprietary lease -- personal property, not real property conveyed by deed
choice_b: By recording a deed at the county clerk's office, exactly as with a house
choice_c: By filing a certificate of occupancy transfer with the local building department
choice_d: Cooperative apartments cannot legally be transferred to a new owner in New York
explanation: Unlike a house or condo (real property conveyed by deed), a cooperative apartment is technically an interest in personal property -- shares of stock in the cooperative corporation, coupled with a proprietary lease for the specific unit -- so a co-op sale closes by assignment of the stock certificate and the proprietary lease, not by delivering a deed.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative housing legal-structure industry practice

question: Why does New York's mortgage recording tax generally NOT apply to a loan used to finance the purchase of cooperative apartment shares?
choice_a: Because a co-op share loan is secured by a UCC-1 financing statement against personal property (the shares/proprietary lease), not by a mortgage against real property, and mortgage recording tax applies only to recorded real property mortgages
choice_b: Because all co-op loans in New York are legally required to be interest-free
choice_c: Because cooperative corporations are exempt from all New York taxation of any kind
choice_d: Because co-op loans are always paid in full at closing with no financing
explanation: A co-op share loan is secured by a UCC-1 financing statement -- a personal property security instrument -- rather than a real property mortgage, because the collateral (co-op shares and the proprietary lease) is personal, not real, property; since mortgage recording tax under NY Tax Law Article 11 applies specifically to recorded real property mortgages, it generally does not apply to co-op share loans.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative housing finance industry practice (UCC-1 financing statement; no mortgage recording tax on personal-property co-op loans)

question: What is the purpose of a 'recognition agreement' between a cooperative corporation and a shareholder's lender?
choice_a: It has the co-op corporation agree to notify the lender before terminating the shareholder's proprietary lease for default, giving the lender an opportunity to cure -- protecting the lender's UCC lien, which is otherwise subordinate to the co-op's own lien for unpaid maintenance
choice_b: It transfers ownership of the co-op corporation itself to the lender
choice_c: It eliminates the shareholder's obligation to pay maintenance
choice_d: It is a document used only in condo transactions, never in co-op transactions
explanation: Because a lender's UCC-1 lien against co-op shares is subordinate to the cooperative corporation's own lien for unpaid maintenance and other charges, lenders require a recognition agreement in which the co-op corporation agrees to notify the lender before terminating the shareholder's proprietary lease for default, giving the lender a chance to cure the default and protect its collateral.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative housing finance industry practice (recognition agreement)

question: How does a cooperative board's approval process for a prospective purchaser typically compare with a condominium's right of first refusal?
choice_a: A co-op board's approval is typically far more discretionary -- the board may reject a prospective purchaser for almost any non-discriminatory reason, often without stating why -- while a condo's right of first refusal is comparatively narrow and, in practice, usually waived
choice_b: Co-op boards have no approval rights whatsoever, unlike condos
choice_c: Condo boards may reject any buyer for any reason with no limits, while co-op boards must approve every applicant
choice_d: Both processes are legally identical in New York, with no meaningful difference
explanation: A cooperative board's approval process is typically much more discretionary than a condominium's right of first refusal -- a co-op board may reject a prospective purchaser for almost any non-discriminatory reason and is generally not required to state a reason, whereas a condo's right of first refusal is narrower in scope and, in practice, is usually waived once the condo declines to exercise it.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative/condominium purchaser-approval industry practice

question: What is a co-op 'flip tax,' and how does it differ from a government transfer tax?
choice_a: A private transfer fee that some cooperative corporations charge a selling shareholder upon resale, authorized by the co-op's proprietary lease/bylaws -- separate from, and in addition to, any government real estate transfer tax
choice_b: A government tax imposed by New York State on all real estate sales, including houses and condos
choice_c: A tax that only applies to commercial office buildings
choice_d: A tax the buyer, never the seller, always pays under state law
explanation: A 'flip tax' is not a government tax at all -- it is a private transfer fee that some cooperative corporations are authorized, under their proprietary lease or bylaws, to charge a selling shareholder on resale (often a percentage of the sale price or profit), separate from and in addition to any government transfer tax that may also apply.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative housing industry practice (co-op flip tax)

question: At a financed cooperative apartment closing, who typically holds the original stock certificate and proprietary lease after closing, until the loan is repaid?
choice_a: The lender, as collateral for the co-op share loan
choice_b: The buyer's real estate broker
choice_c: The county clerk's office
choice_d: The cooperative corporation's managing agent has no involvement, and no one holds these documents
explanation: When a co-op purchase is financed, the lender typically retains the original stock certificate and proprietary lease as collateral securing its loan (paired with its UCC-1 financing statement) until the loan is paid in full, at which point the documents are released to the owner.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY cooperative housing finance industry practice (lender retention of stock certificate/proprietary lease as collateral)

question: How does the mechanism for transferring a condominium unit compare with transferring a cooperative apartment?
choice_a: A condo unit, as real property, is transferred by deed and is eligible for title insurance in the same manner as a house, whereas a co-op is transferred by assignment of stock and proprietary lease and is not conveyed by deed
choice_b: Both are transferred identically, by assignment of corporate stock
choice_c: A condo can never be insured by title insurance
choice_d: A co-op is always transferred by deed, exactly like a condo
explanation: A condominium unit is real property and is conveyed by deed -- like a house -- and is eligible for owner's and lender's title insurance in the same manner as a house, in contrast to a cooperative apartment, which is personal property transferred by stock/lease assignment rather than deed.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY condominium legal-structure industry practice

question: What does a common charge (or maintenance) 'estoppel certificate,' obtained before a condo or co-op closing, confirm?
choice_a: That the seller's common charge/maintenance account is current, with no unpaid arrears, as of a stated date -- information the buyer and title company rely on before closing
choice_b: That the buyer has been formally approved for a mortgage
choice_c: That the property is free of any environmental contamination
choice_d: That the seller has paid all New York State income taxes
explanation: A common charge (condo) or maintenance (co-op) estoppel certificate, obtained from the building's managing agent shortly before closing, confirms the seller's account is current -- with no unpaid arrears -- as of a stated date, protecting the buyer and the title company (in the condo context) from unknowingly assuming the seller's unpaid charges.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY condo/co-op closing industry practice (common charge/maintenance estoppel certificate)

question: What is a key structural reason condo common charges and co-op maintenance often differ in what they cover?
choice_a: A condo owner holds title to, and is separately taxed on, an individual real property unit with no underlying corporate mortgage, so common charges cover only building operating costs -- while a co-op corporation holds title to the entire building (often with a blanket underlying mortgage), so co-op maintenance commonly bundles a pro-rata share of that underlying mortgage debt service and the building's real estate taxes together with operating costs
choice_b: Condo common charges and co-op maintenance are legally required to be identical in every building
choice_c: Co-op maintenance never includes any portion of real estate taxes
choice_d: Condo common charges always include the unit owner's individual mortgage payment
explanation: Because a condo unit owner holds separate title and is separately assessed for real property taxes, condo common charges typically cover only building operating costs; a co-op corporation, by contrast, holds title to the whole building (often subject to a blanket underlying mortgage and a single consolidated tax bill), so co-op maintenance commonly bundles a pro-rata share of that underlying mortgage debt service and real estate taxes together with operating costs -- a structural difference worth understanding when comparing the two.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY condominium/cooperative housing finance structural distinction

question: Mechanically, how does a CEMA (Consolidation, Extension, and Modification Agreement) closing differ from a standard refinance closing?
choice_a: In a CEMA, the existing mortgage is assigned to the new lender and consolidated with the new note/mortgage, rather than being satisfied/discharged and replaced by an entirely new, freestanding mortgage
choice_b: A CEMA always requires the existing mortgage to be paid off and discharged before closing
choice_c: A CEMA eliminates the need for a new lender entirely
choice_d: A CEMA can only be used the very first time a property is ever financed
explanation: Rather than satisfying and discharging the existing mortgage and recording a brand-new one (as in a standard refinance), a CEMA closing has the existing mortgage assigned to the new lender and then consolidated with the new note/mortgage into one obligation -- the mechanical step that allows mortgage recording tax to apply only to the new money advanced.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY CEMA closing-mechanics industry practice

question: Why can arranging a CEMA sometimes extend or complicate a closing timeline compared with a standard refinance?
choice_a: Because it requires the cooperation and document production of the assigning (existing) lender's counsel -- providing mortgage/note copies, assignments, and allonges -- coordination that a standard payoff-and-discharge refinance does not require
choice_b: Because a CEMA legally requires a six-month waiting period before it may close
choice_c: Because CEMAs may only be closed on the last business day of the calendar year
choice_d: Because a CEMA requires approval from the New York State Legislature
explanation: Because a CEMA involves assigning (rather than paying off) the existing mortgage, the new lender's counsel must coordinate with the assigning lender's counsel to obtain and review the existing note, mortgage, and any assignments/allonges, and to prepare the new assignment -- added coordination, dependent on the assigning lender's responsiveness, that a standard payoff-and-discharge refinance does not involve.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY CEMA closing-mechanics industry practice (assigning lender's cooperation/document production)

question: In a 'purchase CEMA' -- used when a buyer's new lender takes an assignment of the seller's existing mortgage rather than requiring it be satisfied -- whose cooperation is additionally needed, beyond what a refinance CEMA requires?
choice_a: The seller's (and the seller's existing lender's), since it is the seller's own existing mortgage being kept alive and assigned to the buyer's new lender rather than paid off and discharged at closing
choice_b: No additional cooperation is ever needed beyond the buyer and buyer's lender
choice_c: Only the county clerk's cooperation is needed
choice_d: Only the buyer's real estate broker's cooperation is needed
explanation: A purchase CEMA keeps the seller's existing mortgage alive (assigning it to the buyer's new lender and consolidating it with the new loan) instead of satisfying and discharging it at closing as in a typical sale -- so it requires the seller's and the seller's existing lender's cooperation, in addition to the buyer's new lender, and is generally arranged well in advance of the closing date rather than at the last minute.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY purchase CEMA closing-mechanics industry practice

question: What is Form TP-584, filed with the deed at a New York closing?
choice_a: The Combined Real Estate Transfer Tax Return and Credit Line Mortgage Certificate, used to report and remit New York State real estate transfer tax
choice_b: An application for a mortgage loan
choice_c: A form used exclusively to apply for STAR property tax relief
choice_d: A form filed only when no attorney represents either party
explanation: Form TP-584, the Combined Real Estate Transfer Tax Return and Credit Line Mortgage Certificate, is filed with the deed at closing to report the transaction and calculate/remit the New York State real estate transfer tax due, and is a standard part of the closing document package.
source_note: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance -- Form TP-584 instructions (Combined Real Estate Transfer Tax Return)

question: What is Form RP-5217, and why does the county clerk require it before recording a deed?
choice_a: The Real Property Transfer Report -- required alongside the deed so the state/local assessment system can track the sale for equalization and assessment purposes; the clerk generally will not record the deed without it
choice_b: A form used only to grieve a property's assessed value
choice_c: A federal form required by the IRS for capital gains reporting
choice_d: A form that replaces the need for a deed entirely
explanation: Form RP-5217, the Real Property Transfer Report, must be filed together with the deed when it is presented for recording, so that state and local assessment offices can track the sale for equalization-rate and assessment purposes; county clerks generally will not accept a deed for recording without a properly completed RP-5217 (or, in New York City, its ACRIS/RP-5217NYC equivalent).
source_note: NYS Office of Real Property Tax Services -- Form RP-5217 filing requirement (Real Property Transfer Report)

question: What is ACRIS, and how is it used in New York City real estate closings?
choice_a: The Automated City Register Information System -- New York City's online system for electronically recording deeds, mortgages, and related documents, and for filing the Real Property Transfer Report, in place of a traditional paper county clerk's office process
choice_b: A statewide database of licensed real estate brokers
choice_c: A New York City rent-stabilization registry
choice_d: A federal system for verifying mortgage interest rates
explanation: ACRIS (the Automated City Register Information System) is New York City's electronic system for recording deeds, mortgages, and other property-related documents, and for filing transfer tax and Real Property Transfer Report information -- functioning in place of the traditional paper-based county clerk recording process used elsewhere in the state.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NYC recording-system industry practice (ACRIS)

question: Why does the closing attorney or title closer prioritize recording the deed and mortgage as soon as possible after a New York closing?
choice_a: Because New York is a 'race-notice' recording jurisdiction (RPL Section 291), under which a later good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who records first can generally take priority over an earlier, unrecorded interest -- so prompt recording protects the new owner/lender's priority
choice_b: Because New York law requires recording within one hour of signing, with no exceptions
choice_c: Recording timing has no legal significance in New York
choice_d: Because recording early avoids having to pay any transfer tax at all
explanation: New York follows a 'race-notice' recording statute (Real Property Law Section 291), meaning a subsequent good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who records first can take priority over an earlier interest that was left unrecorded -- which is why the closing attorney/title closer moves to record the new deed and mortgage as promptly as possible after closing, protecting the buyer's and lender's priority against the 'recording gap' risk.
source_note: NY Real Property Law Section 291 (race-notice recording statute)

question: Given the rise of business-email-compromise scams targeting real estate closings (fraudulent emails purporting to send 'updated wiring instructions'), what best practice is commonly advised before a buyer wires closing funds?
choice_a: Independently verify the wiring instructions by phone, using a phone number obtained from a known, trusted source (not one taken from the email itself), before sending any funds
choice_b: Simply trust any wiring instructions received by email, since email is inherently secure
choice_c: Wire funds to whatever account number appears most recently in any email thread
choice_d: There is no need for any verification, since banks always reverse fraudulent wires automatically
explanation: Because criminals have targeted real estate closings with business-email-compromise scams -- sending fraudulent emails with 'updated' wiring instructions that redirect funds to a scammer's account -- buyers are commonly advised to independently verify wiring instructions by phone, using a number obtained from a trusted source rather than one contained in the email itself, before wiring any closing funds; once wired, such funds are often very difficult or impossible to recover.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated modern closing-practice consumer-protection guidance (wire fraud / business email compromise prevention)

question: At a New York residential closing, remaining heating oil in the seller's tank is typically treated as what, for closing-adjustment purposes?
choice_a: The seller's personal property, which the buyer purchases through a closing credit to the seller based on a tank reading and the current price per gallon -- not something that transfers automatically for free along with the real property
choice_b: Real property that automatically transfers to the buyer for free, with no adjustment
choice_c: An item the seller must always remove entirely before closing, with no purchase option for the buyer
choice_d: An item regulated exclusively by the New York State Liquor Authority
explanation: Remaining heating oil in a tank is treated as the seller's personal property, not an automatic part of the real property conveyance -- so it is customarily handled as a closing adjustment, with the buyer reimbursing the seller for the value of the oil remaining at closing, based on a tank reading (gauge) and the current per-gallon price, rather than transferring for free.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY residential closing-adjustment industry practice (fuel oil proration)

question: At a closing scheduled for March 10, the seller has already paid annual property taxes of $6,205 covering the full calendar year (January 1 - December 31). Using a 365-day proration, with the buyer responsible for taxes starting on the closing date through year-end (297 days, including March 10), how much should the buyer reimburse the seller at closing?
explanation: Daily tax rate = $6,205 / 365 = $17/day exactly. Days from March 10 through December 31, inclusive of March 10, = 297 days. Buyer's reimbursement to seller = 297 x $17 = $5,049.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate closing proration math (applied, illustrative)

question: At a closing scheduled for September 1, the seller has already paid annual property taxes of $10,950 covering the full calendar year (January 1 - December 31). Using a 365-day proration, with the buyer responsible for taxes starting on the closing date through year-end (122 days, including September 1), how much should the buyer reimburse the seller at closing?
explanation: Daily tax rate = $10,950 / 365 = $30/day exactly. Days from September 1 through December 31, inclusive of September 1, = 122 days. Buyer's reimbursement to seller = 122 x $30 = $3,660.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate closing proration math (applied, illustrative)

question: At a closing scheduled for November 20, the seller has already paid annual property taxes of $8,760 covering the full calendar year (January 1 - December 31). Using a 365-day proration, with the buyer responsible for taxes starting on the closing date through year-end (42 days, including November 20), how much should the buyer reimburse the seller at closing?
explanation: Daily tax rate = $8,760 / 365 = $24/day exactly. Days from November 20 through December 31, inclusive of November 20, = 42 days. Buyer's reimbursement to seller = 42 x $24 = $1,008.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate closing proration math (applied, illustrative)

question: New York school district property taxes are billed on a fiscal year running July 1 through June 30 (distinct from the town/county fiscal year, which runs January 1 through December 31). A seller has already paid the full school tax bill of $9,125 for the fiscal year. At an October 5 closing, using a 365-day proration, with the buyer responsible for school taxes from the closing date through the end of the school fiscal year (269 days, including October 5, through June 30), how much should the buyer reimburse the seller at closing?
explanation: Daily school-tax rate = $9,125 / 365 = $25/day exactly. Days from October 5 through June 30 (the end of the school district's July 1 - June 30 fiscal year), inclusive of October 5, = 269 days. Buyer's reimbursement to seller = 269 x $25 = $6,725. Because school and town/county taxes run on different fiscal years in New York, closings commonly involve separate prorations for each.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate closing proration math applied to NY's school district (July 1 - June 30) fiscal year convention

question: A property's calendar-year town/county taxes of $14,600 are billed and payable in arrears (the seller has NOT yet paid any of the current year's tax bill as of closing). At a July 20 closing, using a 365-day proration, the buyer will be responsible for paying the full year's tax bill when it later comes due. Since the seller owned the property for 200 days of the year (January 1 through July 19), what should the seller credit the buyer at closing for the seller's share of the as-yet-unpaid taxes?
explanation: Daily tax rate = $14,600 / 365 = $40/day exactly. The seller owned the property for 200 days (January 1 - July 19, inclusive).
